newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada Supreme Court hears landmark Indian case.
newsitem.headline: Canada Supreme Court hears landmark Indian case.

text.p: Canada's Supreme Court began hearing on Monday a landmark case that will decide whether native Indians' right to their traditional lands was wiped out by colonial rule.

The Gitskan and Wet'suwet'en people claim they are the rightful owners of 22,000 square miles (57,000 sq km) of land in remote northwestern British Columbia because they never signed treaties with British settlers.
The area in dispute is more than twice the size of the U.S. state of Massachusetts and rich in resources including timber, fish, natural gas and minerals.
"This is the most significant Indian rights case ever to come before the Supreme Court," said Paul Tennant, a native affairs expert at the University of British Columbia.
The Supreme Court hearing in Ottawa is scheduled to last two days and a decision is not expected before the autumn at the earliest.
The case was lodged in 1984 by 51 hereditary chiefs of the two bands against the governments of British Columbia and Canada and has slowly made its way through lower courts.

The Indians contend they should have the right to govern their own affairs and allocate fishing, mining, water and forestry rights in their area. The bands' roughly 6,000 members now largely live on reserves where unemployment and other social ills are endemic.
"Those lands were stolen from us. In our opinion, our rights to those lands have never been extinguished," said Herb George, speaker for the Wet'suet'en hereditary chiefs.
"We want an order from the Supreme Court recognising our title still exists and the nature and scope of that title and our governance rights."

British Columbia is opposing the Indians' efforts to gain sweeping title to the land, arguing that any exclusive rights were erased when the territory joined Canada in 1871. The province is willing to recognise some self-government rights.
The province has been the main counterparty in the case and Canada's federal government has taken part primarily for procedural reasons.

A lower court ruled in 1991 that the natives lost title to the land by virtue of colonial settlement and rule in the 19th century. An appeal court later overturned parts of the decision, saying the natives had some non-exclusive rights to about half of the area they originally claimed.

Legal and native affairs experts said the ultimate Supreme Court ruling will have sweeping ramifications. The judgment will determine to what degree Indians still have rights over traditional lands not covered by treaties and their inherent right to self government.

A host of groups representing mining, timber, fishing and ranching interests are intervening in the case to support the government. Native Indian bands and groups are intervening on behalf of the two bands.

Although the Indians have said they would not seek to take over land that is owned privately, the case has raised concern among some residents in the region who fear it could cause economic and social upheaval.

"It would be just total chaos if the Supreme Court reversed the lower court ruling ... It's fair to say it would throw the entire economy of northwest British Columbia into a real tailspin," said Mike Scott, a member of parliament from the area and a critic of the Indians' effort.
